stem: What is the main advantage of a distribution-free (nonparametric) test over a parametric one?
correct: Validity does not rest on a distributional family such as the normal.
It stays valid when normality fails.

distractors.text: It always has greater power than the parametric test.
distractors.misconception: ignores that power can be lower when the parametric model holds

distractors.text: It needs no assumptions at all, not even independence.
It uses the actual values of the data more fully than a parametric test.
It works only for categorical data.
It gives estimates with smaller variance in every case.

explanation: Rank tests keep the stated significance level whatever the continuous distribution; the price is a small loss of power when the parametric model is exactly right.

stem: How does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test compare in efficiency with the one-sample $t$ test?
correct: Its efficiency is $3/\pi$ under normality and can exceed 1 for heavy tails.
It loses little power for normal data.

distractors.text: It is always far less efficient than the $t$ test.
distractors.misconception: ignores the high efficiency under normality

distractors.text: It is always more efficient than the $t$ test.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the $t$ test is best under normality

distractors.text: Its efficiency is exactly 1 for every distribution.
It has an efficiency of zero for symmetric data.
Efficiency comparisons are impossible because the tests use different statistics.

explanation: The ARE of the Wilcoxon test relative to the $t$ test never falls below 0.864 for any continuous distribution, which makes it a safe choice.

stem: A test is called distribution-free. What does that guarantee about its null distribution?
correct: The null distribution is the same for every continuous distribution the data may have.
One table of critical values serves every continuous population, whatever its shape.

distractors.text: The test is equally powerful whatever population the data come from, since ranks hide the shape.
distractors.misconception: confuses validity of the null distribution with power

distractors.text: No assumption of any kind is needed about the data, not even independence or continuity.
distractors.misconception: forgets the assumptions that remain, such as independent observations

distractors.text: The null distribution is normal for every sample size, because the statistic is based on ranks.
Ties and discrete data have no effect, because ranks replace the raw observations.
distractors.misconception: ignores the effect of ties on rank tests

distractors.text: The p-value is exact for any sample size even when observations are dependent on one another.

explanation: Distribution-free means the null distribution does not depend on the (continuous) population. Independence and continuity (no ties) are still assumed, and power does depend on the population.

stem: When the data are normal, how does a rank-based test such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test compare with the $t$ test?
correct: It loses little: its asymptotic relative efficiency against the $t$ test is $3/\pi\approx0.955$.
It needs only about $5\%$ more observations than the $t$ test to reach the same power.

distractors.text: It is far less efficient, needing about twice as many observations for the same power.
distractors.misconception: overstates the cost of using ranks

distractors.text: It is more efficient, because ranks remove the influence of the tails of the normal curve.
distractors.misconception: thinks ranks beat the exactly optimal test under normality

distractors.text: It has exactly the same power, because the ranks of normal data are themselves normal.
distractors.misconception: assumes no loss of information from ranking

distractors.text: It cannot be used, because rank tests require the data to be clearly non-normal.
distractors.misconception: thinks rank tests need non-normal data

distractors.text: Its loss grows without bound as the sample size increases, because ranks discard the sizes.
distractors.misconception: confuses a constant efficiency loss with an unbounded one

explanation: Under normality the Wilcoxon signed-rank test has ARE $3/\pi$ against the $t$ test, so the price of using ranks is small; for heavy-tailed data the ARE is at least $0.864$ and can exceed $1$.

stem: For which kind of population is a nonparametric test most clearly preferable to the $t$ test?
correct: A heavy-tailed population, where outliers make the mean unstable and a rank test is more efficient.
The double exponential, where the sign test needs only half the observations.

distractors.text: A normal population with a very small sample, because rank tests are exact for small normal samples.
distractors.misconception: thinks small normal samples favour rank tests

distractors.text: Any population with a large sample, because the central limit theorem does not apply to ranks.
distractors.misconception: thinks the CLT fails for large samples

distractors.text: A population with known variance, because only the $t$ test needs the variance estimated.
distractors.misconception: confuses the known-variance z test with the choice of method

distractors.text: A uniform population, because the $t$ test is not valid for bounded data.
distractors.misconception: thinks boundedness invalidates the t test

distractors.text: A population with no ties, because rank methods cannot be used when any value repeats.
distractors.misconception: thinks ties make rank methods unusable

explanation: Heavy tails make the sample mean erratic. For the double exponential the sign test has ARE $2$ against the $t$ test, so it needs about half as many observations.

stem: What does the sign test for a hypothesised median $\theta_0$ count?
correct: The observations above $\theta_0$, out of those that differ from $\theta_0$; under $H_0$ the count is binomial with $p=\tfrac12$.
How many differences $X_i-\theta_0$ are positive among the nonzero ones, a $\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)$ count under $H_0$.

distractors.text: The sum of the ranks of the observations that lie above $\theta_0$, which has a signed-rank null distribution.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sign test with the signed-rank test

distractors.text: How many observations are below the sample mean, which is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)$ for any distribution.
distractors.misconception: uses the sample mean instead of the hypothesised median

distractors.text: The number of observations at least $\theta_0$ out of all $n$, including those equal to $\theta_0$, as $\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)$.
distractors.misconception: keeps ties in the count and in n

distractors.text: The standardised difference between $\bar x$ and $\theta_0$, which is approximately normal.
distractors.misconception: describes a z or t test

distractors.text: The number of runs of consecutive observations on the same side of $\theta_0$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sign test with a runs test

explanation: Drop observations equal to $\theta_0$, let $n$ be the number left and $B$ the number above $\theta_0$. Under $H_0$, $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)$.

stem: Some observations equal the hypothesised median $\theta_0$. How does the sign test treat them?
correct: They are dropped and $n$ is reduced to the number of observations that differ from $\theta_0$.
Observations equal to $\theta_0$ carry no sign, so they are removed before the binomial calculation.

distractors.text: They are counted as positive, so the test becomes conservative against the alternative.
Half of them are counted as positive and half as negative, so $B$ may stay as a half-integer.
distractors.misconception: splits ties and keeps them in n

distractors.text: They are counted as negative, so that the test is conservative for the upper alternative.
distractors.misconception: assigns ties to the other side

distractors.text: They make the test invalid, which cannot be used on a sample containing any such value.
distractors.misconception: thinks ties rule the test out entirely

distractors.text: They are replaced by the sample median, so $n$ stays the same and the count is unchanged.

explanation: A value equal to $\theta_0$ is neither above nor below it, so it carries no information about the sign; drop it and use the smaller $n$.

stem: A two-sided sign test has $B$ observations above the median out of $n$. How is the exact p-value found?
correct: Double the smaller of the two tail probabilities $P(B'\ge B)$ and $P(B'\le B)$, capping the result at $1$.
Twice the smaller tail probability, never above $1$.

distractors.text: Use $P(B'=B)$, the probability of exactly the observed count, as the p-value.
distractors.misconception: uses a point probability instead of a tail

distractors.text: Double the larger of the two tail probabilities so that the test errs on the safe side.
Use the upper tail $P(B'\ge B)$ without doubling, because the binomial is symmetric.
distractors.misconception: forgets that two-sided needs both tails

distractors.text: Use the normal approximation, which gives the exact p-value for every sample size.
Add $P(B'\ge B)$ and $P(B'\le B)$, which together always count the observed value twice.

explanation: For $H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0$ both tails count. Since $\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)$ is symmetric the two-sided p-value is twice the smaller tail (at most $1$).

stem: Why can the sign test be applied to data from any continuous distribution?
correct: Under $H_0$ each observation exceeds the median with probability $\tfrac12$, whatever the distribution.
The count above the median is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)$ for every continuous law.

distractors.text: It is based on the mean, which exists for every continuous distribution.
distractors.misconception: confuses the median with the mean

distractors.text: For a continuous distribution the sizes of all the differences are equal, so only signs matter.
distractors.misconception: invents a property of continuous distributions

distractors.text: The central limit theorem makes the count normal for every sample size.
distractors.misconception: thinks the null distribution is only asymptotic

distractors.text: It assumes symmetry about the median, which every continuous distribution has.
distractors.misconception: assumes symmetry, which the sign test does not need

distractors.text: Ranks of the data are uniform for every sample, so the statistic is uniform.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sign count with rank statistics

explanation: By definition of the median, $P(X>\theta)=\tfrac12$ for a continuous distribution, so the sign count is binomial and symmetry is not required.

stem: How does the power of the sign test compare with that of the $t$ test?
correct: About $\pi/2\approx1.57$ times the observations under normality, but fewer for heavy-tailed data.
Less efficient under normality (ARE $2/\pi$), more efficient under the double exponential.

distractors.text: It is always as powerful as the $t$ test, because both of them test the centre of the distribution.
distractors.misconception: assumes equal power because both test location

distractors.text: It is always more powerful, because ignoring the sizes protects it against outliers.
It is less powerful for every distribution, because it discards the sizes of the observations.
distractors.misconception: ignores heavy-tailed cases where it wins

distractors.text: It has ARE $3/\pi$ against the $t$ test, the same as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
distractors.misconception: confuses sign test with signed-rank efficiency

distractors.text: Its power does not depend on the sample size, since only the signs enter the statistic.
distractors.misconception: thinks power does not grow with n

explanation: Under normality the sign test has ARE $2/\pi$ against the $t$ test; under the double exponential its ARE is $2$.

stem: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent with a common continuous cdf $F$. What is the cdf of the sample maximum $X_{(n)}$?
correct: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^n$, since all $n$ observations must be at most $x$.
It is $F(x)$ multiplied by itself $n$ times, one factor per observation.

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=nF(x)$ for $x$ in the support, with one term for each observation.
distractors.misconception: adds the probabilities instead of multiplying them

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=1-(1-F(x))^n$, because one observation below $x$ is enough.
distractors.misconception: gives the cdf of the minimum instead

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)$, so the maximum has the same law as a single draw.
distractors.misconception: thinks the maximum has the same law as one observation

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^{1/n}$, which rises as the sample size grows.
$P(X_{(n)}\le x)=1-F(x)^n$, the chance that all observations exceed $x$.
distractors.misconception: confuses all below with all above

explanation: The maximum is at most $x$ exactly when each of the $n$ independent observations is, which gives $F(x)^n$. The minimum has cdf $1-(1-F(x))^n$.

stem: For $n$ independent continuous observations, which statement correctly describes $P(X_{(k)}\le x)$, where $F=F(x)$ and $1\le k\le n$?
correct: It is the chance that at least $k$ observations are at most $x$, $\sum_{j=k}^{n}\binom nj F^j(1-F)^{n-j}$.
With $N\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,F)$ the number at most $x$, it equals $P(N\ge k)$.

distractors.text: It is $\binom nk F^k(1-F)^{n-k}$, the probability that exactly $k$ observations lie below $x$.
distractors.misconception: uses exactly $k$ instead of at least $k$

distractors.text: It is $\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom nj F^j(1-F)^{n-j}$, the probability of at most $k$ observations below $x$.
distractors.misconception: flips the direction of the binomial tail

distractors.text: It is $F^k$, because the $k$ smallest observations must all lie below the point $x$.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the other observations are free and which ones are below

distractors.text: It is $kF(x)/n$, a linear interpolation between the minimum and the maximum of the sample.
distractors.misconception: treats order statistics as proportional to the cdf

distractors.text: It is $F^k(1-F)^{n-k}$, with no binomial coefficient needed for the choice of observations.
distractors.misconception: forgets the number of ways to choose which observations are below

explanation: $X_{(k)}\le x$ exactly when at least $k$ observations are at most $x$, and that count is binomial. For $k=n$ this reduces to $F^n$.

stem: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid with a continuous cdf $F$, and let $R_i$ be the rank of $X_i$ in the sample. Which statement is true?
correct: The rank vector is uniform over all $n!$ permutations, whatever $F$ is.
Each assignment of the ranks $1,\dots,n$ to the observations has probability $1/n!$, free of $F$.

distractors.text: The law of the ranks depends on $F$, so rank procedures need $F$ to be known beforehand.
distractors.misconception: thinks ranks carry the shape of the distribution

distractors.text: Each $R_i$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ only when $F$ is symmetric about its centre.
distractors.misconception: believes symmetry is needed for rank laws to be free of $F$

distractors.text: The ranks are independent of each other, because the observations themselves are independent.
distractors.misconception: misses that the ranks always sum to a fixed total

distractors.text: The largest rank is more likely to go to an observation that falls far out in a tail.
distractors.misconception: confuses the size of a value with its rank

distractors.text: The ranks are uniform over the permutations only when the data come from a normal law.
distractors.misconception: ties distribution-free behaviour to the normal law

explanation: Continuity rules out ties and exchangeability makes every ordering equally likely. The ranks are not independent: they always sum to $n(n+1)/2$.

stem: A distribution-free confidence interval for the $p$-quantile $\xi_p$ of a continuous distribution is $(X_{(r)},X_{(s)})$ with $r<s$. How is its coverage found?
correct: It is $P(r\le B\le s-1)$ with $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, whatever $F$ is.
It is the chance that the binomial count of observations below $\xi_p$ lies in $[r,s-1]$.

distractors.text: It requires $F$ to be normal, since the endpoints are order statistics of the data.
distractors.misconception: thinks order statistics need a parametric model

distractors.text: It is $(s-r)/n$, the fraction of the sample lying between the two endpoints of the interval.
distractors.misconception: confuses coverage of the quantile with the sample fraction

distractors.text: It is $P(B\ge r)$ with $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,1/2)$, whatever the value of $p$ is.
distractors.misconception: uses the median probability for every quantile

distractors.text: It tends to 1 as $n$ grows, even when $r$ and $s$ are held fixed.
distractors.misconception: believes more data always raises the coverage of fixed order statistics

distractors.text: It can be made exactly $1-\alpha$ for any chosen level $\alpha$ and any sample size.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the coverage takes only discrete binomial values

explanation: Since $F(\xi_p)=p$, the count of observations below $\xi_p$ is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, whatever $F$ is. Because the count is discrete, one picks $r,s$ with coverage at least $1-\alpha$.

stem: How can a confidence interval for the population cdf value $F(x_0)$ be obtained?
correct: The count of observations at most $x_0$ is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,F(x_0))$, so a binomial-proportion interval applies to $\hat F(x_0)$.
$\hat F(x_0)$ is a sample proportion, so the usual interval for a binomial proportion can be used.

distractors.text: Use the $t$ interval for the mean of the observations, since $F(x_0)$ is a population mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses a probability with a mean

distractors.text: Use the order-statistic interval $(X_{(r)},X_{(s)})$, which covers $F(x_0)$ with a fixed probability.
distractors.misconception: applies the median interval to a cdf value

distractors.text: The empirical cdf is normal with variance $1/n$ for every $F$ and every $x_0$.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the variance depends on $F(x_0)$

distractors.text: Use the Kolmogorov-Smirnov critical value, which applies to a single point in the same way.
distractors.misconception: uses a simultaneous band for one point

distractors.text: It cannot be done without assuming a parametric family for the distribution function.

explanation: At a fixed $x_0$, $n\hat F(x_0)\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,F(x_0))$, so $\hat F\pm z\sqrt{\hat F(1-\hat F)/n}$ is an approximate interval.

stem: What assumption makes a permutation test valid?
correct: Under $H_0$ the labels are exchangeable.
All relabellings are equally likely.

distractors.text: The data are normally distributed.
The sample is large.
The variances are known.
The observations are paired.
Only the order of the observations matters.

explanation: Exchangeability can fail with unequal variances between groups or dependent data, in which case a plain permutation test can be invalid.

stem: How is an exact permutation p-value computed for a difference in group means?
correct: Enumerate all assignments and find the share at least as extreme.
The share of relabellings with a gap as large as observed.

distractors.text: By comparing the statistic with a normal distribution.
By resampling the data with replacement.
By dividing the observed difference by its estimated standard error.
By counting the sign changes.
By using only the observed assignment.

explanation: With groups of sizes $n_1,n_2$ there are $\binom{n_1+n_2}{n_1}$ assignments; the observed one is included, so the smallest p-value is $1/\binom{n}{n_1}$.

stem: How many distinct assignments exist when $m$ of $N$ units are randomly assigned to treatment?
correct: $\binom Nm$, as order within groups is irrelevant.
Ways to choose the treated units.

distractors.text: $N!$, counting every ordering of the units.
$2^N$, counting all binary labellings.
distractors.misconception: counts labellings that ignore the group sizes

distractors.text: $m!\,(N-m)!$, a product of factorials.
$N\cdot m$, the product of the sizes.
$\binom Nm/2$, halving for symmetry.

explanation: The number of assignments sets the smallest attainable p-value, $1/\binom Nm$, so small experiments can have limited resolution.

stem: What is a Monte Carlo permutation test?
correct: It approximates the permutation distribution with random relabellings.
Random permutations estimate the $p$-value.

distractors.text: It gives exactly the same value as enumeration for any number of draws.
It resamples data with replacement.
It requires a parametric model.
It cannot be used for large samples.
It uses the normal approximation.

explanation: A p-value estimate $(1+\#\{T^*\ge T_{obs}\})/(1+B)$ with $B$ random permutations remains valid.

stem: What is an advantage of permutation tests over $t$ tests?
correct: Exact validity in finite samples under exchangeability.
Any test statistic can be used.

distractors.text: They always have more power.
They need no assumption at all.
They are faster to compute.
They estimate the effect size more accurately.
They work for any dependence structure.

explanation: For the difference in means with many observations, the permutation test is close to the $t$ test, but it also allows medians, trimmed means or ranks.

stem: What does the Mann-Whitney (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test compare?
correct: Two independent samples, through pooled ranks.
Whether $P(X>Y)=1/2$.

distractors.text: Two paired samples through the signs of the differences.
The means of two samples, assuming normality.
The variances of two samples.
Two proportions.
Three or more groups.

explanation: If the two distributions differ only by a shift, the test is a test of equal medians; in general it tests stochastic dominance.

stem: How is the Mann-Whitney statistic $U$ related to the rank sum $W$ of sample 1 (sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$)?

distractors.misconception: confuses with the other sample's statistic

distractors.text: $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independent.

explanation: The smallest rank sum possible is $n_1(n_1+1)/2$, when sample 1 holds the lowest ranks, which gives $U_1=0$.

stem: What are the mean and variance of $U$ under $H_0$ for sample sizes $n_1,n_2$ (no ties)?

distractors.text: Mean $n_1n_2$ and variance $n_1n_2(n_1+n_2)/12$.
Mean $n_1n_2/2$ and variance $n_1n_2/4$.
Mean $(n_1+n_2)/2$ and variance $(n_1+n_2)/12$.
distractors.misconception: uses the total sample size only

distractors.text: Mean $0$ and variance $1$.
Mean $n_1n_2/2$ and variance $n_1n_2(n_1+n_2+1)/6$.

explanation: These give $z=(U-n_1n_2/2)/\sqrt{n_1n_2(n_1+n_2+1)/12}$, with a tie correction to the variance if needed.

stem: What does the quantity $U_1/(n_1n_2)$ estimate?
correct: The chance a random observation of sample 1 beats one of sample 2.
The probabilistic index $P(X>Y)$.

distractors.text: The difference in medians.
The ratio of the two sample means.
The correlation between the two samples.
The significance level of the test.
The probability that the two samples are equal.

explanation: A value of 0.5 means no tendency; values near 1 mean sample 1 almost always exceeds sample 2. It is also the area under the ROC curve.

stem: How are ties handled in the Mann-Whitney test?
correct: Ties get average ranks, and the variance gets a correction.
Mid-ranks are used.

distractors.text: Tied observations are removed from the sample.
Ties are always assigned the lowest rank.
Ties are not possible for continuous data, so they can be ignored in practice.
Ties are broken in favour of the larger sample.
Ties make the test invalid.

explanation: With many ties (such as ordinal ratings), the normal approximation with the tie correction is used instead of exact tables.

stem: What does the Hodges-Lehmann estimator of the shift $\Delta$ between two samples compute?
correct: The median of all $mn$ pairwise differences $X_i-Y_j$.
The shift for which the Mann-Whitney statistic equals its null mean, found from the pairwise differences.

distractors.text: The difference between the two sample means.
The difference between the two sample medians.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the difference of medians

distractors.text: The mean of all pairwise differences $X_i-Y_j$, which equals the difference of means.
distractors.misconception: uses the mean of the differences instead of the median

distractors.text: The median of the differences of the ranks of the two samples.
The average of the smallest and largest pairwise difference.
distractors.misconception: uses the midrange of the differences

explanation: The Hodges-Lehmann estimate is the median of the $mn$ differences; it inherits the robustness of the Mann-Whitney test and differs from $\bar x-\bar y$.

stem: How is a confidence interval for the shift $\Delta$ built from the Mann-Whitney test?
correct: The $k$-th smallest and $k$-th largest of the $mn$ pairwise differences, with $k$ from the null law of $U$.
Order statistics of the pairwise differences, set by the Mann-Whitney critical value.

distractors.text: Take the difference in sample means plus and minus $t$ quantiles times the pooled standard error.
Take order statistics of the pooled sample of all $m+n$ observations.
distractors.misconception: uses the pooled sample instead of the differences

distractors.text: Take the bootstrap percentiles of the difference in sample means only.
Invert the sign test applied to the paired differences of the two samples.
distractors.misconception: applies the paired-sample method to independent samples

distractors.text: Take the values of $\Delta$ for which the rank sum of $X$ equals its null mean exactly.
distractors.misconception: uses a single value instead of an acceptance region

explanation: Inverting the Mann-Whitney test gives an interval whose ends are the $k$-th smallest and $k$-th largest of the $mn$ pairwise differences.

stem: What do the Siegel-Tukey and Ansari-Bradley tests compare for two samples that share the same location?
correct: The dispersion of the two populations, using ranks that are small for extreme observations.
Which sample is more spread out, judged through rank sums of the pooled data.

distractors.text: The medians of the two populations, using the ordinary Wilcoxon ranks of the pooled data.
distractors.misconception: confuses scale tests with location tests

distractors.text: Whether the two distribution functions differ anywhere, using the largest vertical gap.
The means of the two populations, assuming that the two variances are equal.
The correlation between two paired variables, using the ranks within each variable.
Only the tail probabilities of the pooled sample, ignoring the centre of the data.

explanation: Both tests turn a difference in spread into a difference in rank sums by giving low ranks to extreme observations.

stem: How are ranks assigned to the sorted combined sample in the Siegel-Tukey test?
correct: Rank $1$ to the smallest value, $2$ and $3$ to the two largest, $4$ and $5$ to the next two smallest, and so on.
Ranks run inwards from both ends, so central values get the highest ranks.

distractors.text: Ranks increase steadily from the smallest to the largest value, exactly as in the rank-sum test.
Rank $1$ goes to the median and ranks grow outwards, so the extreme values receive the highest ranks.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the scoring

distractors.text: Each sample is ranked separately and the two sets of ranks are then compared directly.
distractors.misconception: ranks within samples instead of the pooled data

distractors.text: Ranks depend on the absolute size of each observation and ignore which sample it came from.
Ranks $1$ and $2$ go to the two largest values and $3$ to the smallest, then the pattern repeats.

explanation: Siegel-Tukey scores run $1;\,2,3;\,4,5;\dots$ alternately from the low and high ends, so extreme observations get small scores and a small rank sum for $X$ suggests larger spread.

stem: Why do the Siegel-Tukey and Ansari-Bradley tests need the two samples to share a location?
correct: If the centres differ, a location shift changes the rank pattern and is mistaken for a scale difference.
A shift in centre confounds the ranks used to measure scale.

distractors.text: The ranks cannot be computed unless the two sample medians are exactly equal.
distractors.misconception: thinks the ranks need equal medians to exist

distractors.text: The null distribution is only defined when the two sample sizes are equal.
distractors.misconception: confuses the location assumption with equal sizes

distractors.text: Scale differences cannot exist unless the centres differ, so equal centres mean no information.
Ties are impossible unless the two locations are the same, and ties break the tests.
The F test on variances needs equal centres but a rank test does not, so the assumption is spurious.

explanation: With unequal medians one can first subtract each sample's median (or use the deviance-based RMD test), so that location differences do not masquerade as scale differences.

stem: How does the ratio of mean deviances (RMD) test compare the scales of two samples?
correct: Divide the mean absolute deviation from the median of $X$ by that of $Y$, and judge the ratio by a permutation test.
The mean absolute deviations about each sample's median are compared as a ratio, with a permutation null distribution.

distractors.text: Divide the two sample variances and compare the ratio with an $F$ distribution on $m-1$ and $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
Divide the two sample medians and judge the ratio by a normal approximation.
Rank the absolute deviations and sum the ranks of $X$ using the Wilcoxon table.
Use the ratio of the interquartile ranges as a pivot whose null distribution is known exactly.
Compare the means of the squared deviations by a paired $t$ test.

explanation: RMD uses absolute deviations about the median (robust to non-normality) and gets its null distribution by permuting the data between the two samples.

stem: Why is the $F$ test for equal variances unreliable for non-normal data?
correct: Its null distribution relies on normality, and with heavy tails it rejects a true null too often.
The variance ratio is no longer $F$ distributed for non-normal data.

distractors.text: It has too little power under normality compared with any rank test.
distractors.misconception: confuses a validity problem with a power problem

distractors.text: It compares the means rather than the variances, so it answers the wrong question.
It needs equal sample sizes, which non-normal data cannot provide.
Variances do not exist for any non-normal distribution, so the ratio is undefined.
distractors.misconception: thinks variances only exist for the normal

distractors.text: The ratio of ranks cannot be computed, so the F test cannot be carried out.
distractors.misconception: confuses the F test with rank methods

explanation: The $F$ test for a variance ratio is very sensitive to kurtosis: with non-normal data its true size can be far above the nominal level, which motivates permutation and rank tests.

stem: What is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic for testing $H_0:F=F_0$?
correct: $D_n=\sup_x|F_n(x)-F_0(x)|$, the largest vertical gap.
The maximum gap between empirical and claimed cdfs.

distractors.text: The sum of squared differences between $F_n$ and $F_0$.
The difference between the sample mean and the hypothesised mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a test of the mean

distractors.text: The difference of the sample medians.
The area between $F_n$ and $F_0$.
The difference between the largest and smallest observations.

explanation: Compute from the ordered sample: $D_n=\max_i\max\{i/n-F_0(x_{(i)}),\ F_0(x_{(i)})-(i-1)/n\}$.

stem: When is the null distribution of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic free of the underlying distribution?
correct: When $F_0$ is continuous and fully specified.
Critical values do not depend on which.

distractors.text: For any $F_0$, including discrete ones.
When the parameters of $F_0$ are estimated from the same data.
Only when the data are normal.
Only for samples of size one.
Never, since it always depends on the distribution.

explanation: If parameters are estimated (the normal with estimated mean and variance), use Lilliefors' modified critical values, which are smaller.

stem: Why is the Anderson-Darling test often more powerful than the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against tail alternatives?
correct: It weights the tails more heavily.
It stresses tail discrepancies.

distractors.text: It ignores the tails entirely.
It uses only the median.
It is a rank test based on signs.
It does not need a specified distribution.
distractors.misconception: ignores that it tests a null distribution

distractors.text: It uses the largest vertical distance.

explanation: The statistic integrates $(F_n-F_0)^2/\{F_0(1-F_0)\}$, which blows up in the tails and so detects heavy tails. For financial returns tail fit matters.

stem: What does the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compare?
correct: Largest gap between two empirical cdfs.
Whether two samples differ.

distractors.text: The means of the two samples.
The variances of the two samples.
The ranks of paired observations.
Only the medians of the two samples.
The sample with the more extreme minimum.

explanation: It is sensitive to differences in location, scale or shape, but most sensitive around the centre of the distributions.

stem: How should a result of a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with a very large sample be read?
correct: Even a tiny departure can be significant.
The test detects negligible deviations.

distractors.text: A significant result always means the departure is large.
Large samples make the test lose power.
The test is invalid for large samples.
The $p$-value is independent of the sample size.
Nonsignificance proves that $F=F_0$.
distractors.misconception: confuses with proof of the null

explanation: $\sqrt nD_n$ is compared with the Kolmogorov distribution; the 5% point is about 1.36, so $D_n>1.36/\sqrt n$ rejects.

stem: What does the Kruskal-Wallis test do?
correct: Whether $k$ independent samples share a distribution, using pooled ranks.
The rank version of one-way ANOVA.

distractors.text: It compares paired measurements with signs.
It tests the equality of $k$ variances.
It tests for a trend over time.
It compares two samples only.
It requires normality in each group.

explanation: A significant result says that at least one group differs; post-hoc pairwise tests (Dunn) show which.

stem: How is the Kruskal-Wallis statistic computed?
correct: $H=\frac{12}{N(N+1)}\sum_i R_i^2/n_i-3(N+1)$, compared with $\chi^2_{k-1}$.
From group rank sums.

distractors.text: $H=\sum_i(\bar R_i-\bar R)$, compared with $\chi^2_{k}$.
distractors.misconception: gives a statistic summing to zero with wrong degrees of freedom

distractors.text: $H=\sum_in_i\bar x_i$, compared with a normal distribution.
From the largest and the smallest group means.
$H$ is compared with $\chi^2_{N-1}$.
distractors.misconception: uses the wrong degrees of freedom

distractors.text: $H$ uses the raw observations, not ranks, and is compared with a $t$ distribution.

explanation: Under $H_0$ every group has expected rank sum $n_i(N+1)/2$, and $H$ measures deviations from it.

stem: What are the large-sample null distributions of the Kruskal-Wallis and Friedman statistics?
correct: Both are approximately $\chi^2$ with $k-1$ degrees of freedom.
One fewer than the number of groups.

distractors.text: Both are approximately standard normal.
Chi-square with $N-1$ degrees of freedom.
Chi-square with $k$ degrees of freedom.
An $F$ distribution with $(k-1,N-k)$ degrees of freedom.
Uniform on $[0,1]$.

explanation: For small samples exact permutation tables are used. A significant result calls for pairwise follow-up tests with a multiplicity correction.

stem: What is the idea of the permutation $F$ test for $k$ groups?
correct: Recompute $F$ over relabellings of the pooled data and compare the observed $F$ with that permutation distribution.
The null distribution of $F$ is built by permuting the group labels, so no normality is assumed.

distractors.text: Replace the data by ranks and use the $F$ table with $k-1$ and $N-k$ degrees of freedom.
Permute only within groups, so that the group means stay the same in every permutation.
distractors.misconception: permutes within groups, which changes nothing

distractors.text: Use the normal-theory $F$ distribution and permute only for the follow-up pairwise comparisons.
distractors.misconception: limits permutation to post hoc tests

distractors.text: Sort each group and compare the observed $F$ with $F_{k-1,N-k}$ after sorting.
Permute across groups but let the group sizes vary at random from one permutation to the next.
distractors.misconception: changes the group sizes in the permutation

explanation: Under $H_0$ the $N$ observations are exchangeable across groups, so $F$ can be recomputed for all (or many random) assignments of the observations to groups of the original sizes.

stem: How are tied values handled in the Kruskal-Wallis statistic?
correct: Tied values receive mid-ranks and the statistic is divided by $1-\sum(t^3-t)/(N^3-N)$.
Average ranks are used and the statistic is inflated by dividing by the tie correction factor.

distractors.text: Tied observations are dropped and $N$ is reduced accordingly.
distractors.misconception: removes ties instead of using mid-ranks

distractors.text: Ties are broken at random, which leaves the statistic exactly the same as without ties.
Tied values receive the smallest rank of their group and no correction is applied.
distractors.misconception: uses minimum ranks and no correction

distractors.text: The statistic is multiplied by $1-\sum(t^3-t)/(N^3-N)$, which makes it smaller.
The test cannot be used whenever any value occurs more than once in the combined data.
distractors.misconception: thinks any tie rules the test out

explanation: With ties the ranks are averaged and $KW_{\text{ties}}=KW/C$ where $C=1-\sum(t^3-t)/(N^3-N)<1$, so the correction increases the statistic.

stem: Why does running every pairwise test at level $\alpha$ inflate the Type I error of the whole analysis?
correct: The chance of at least one false rejection among many tests, the family-wise error rate, exceeds $\alpha$.
Each true null can be rejected, so false rejections accumulate across tests.

distractors.text: Pairwise tests are always biased towards rejection because each one uses fewer observations.
The type II error shrinks with every extra test, which raises the type I error.
Because the tests share observations, each individual p-value is invalid on its own.
Only the omnibus test has a valid null distribution, so pairwise tests have none.
distractors.misconception: denies a null distribution for pairwise tests

distractors.text: Because the number of pairs $k(k-1)/2$ is always even, rejections come in pairs.

explanation: With $m$ independent true nulls tested at level $\alpha$ the chance of at least one false rejection is $1-(1-\alpha)^m$, which exceeds $\alpha$ for $m\ge2$.

stem: How does the Bonferroni adjustment control the family-wise error rate for $m$ comparisons?
correct: Each test is run at level $\alpha/m$, and the union bound keeps the overall error rate at most $\alpha$.
Using level $\alpha/m$ per comparison makes the individual error rates add up to at most $\alpha$.

distractors.text: Each test is run at level $m\alpha$ so that rejections become rarer as comparisons are added.
The p-values are divided by $m$ and then compared with the unadjusted level $\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: divides the p-values instead of the level

distractors.text: Only the largest difference is tested, at level $\alpha$, which is equivalent to Tukey's method.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a range-based method

distractors.text: It guarantees power $1-\alpha$ for each comparison, whatever the sample sizes are.
It is exact, and not conservative, whenever the $m$ tests are dependent.

explanation: By the union bound, $P(\cup E_j)\le\sum P(E_j)\le m\cdot\alpha/m=\alpha$. The price is conservativeness, which grows with $m$.

stem: How do Fisher's LSD and Tukey's HSD multiple comparison procedures differ?
correct: LSD does not control the family-wise error rate, while HSD controls it exactly with equal sample sizes.
HSD uses the studentised range; LSD only protects by a prior omnibus test.

distractors.text: LSD is more conservative than HSD, because it adjusts the level for the number of pairs.
distractors.misconception: swaps the conservativeness of the two

distractors.text: HSD can only be used on ranks, while LSD can only be used on the raw data.
distractors.misconception: restricts each method to one data type

distractors.text: They are the same procedure under different names, and always declare the same pairs different.
LSD is exact for unequal sample sizes while HSD requires every group to be the same size.
distractors.misconception: reverses the role of unequal sizes

distractors.text: HSD requires a significant omnibus test first, but LSD can be used without one.

explanation: LSD is 'protected' by the omnibus test but each pairwise test is at level $\alpha$; HSD compares all pairs with the null distribution of the largest mean difference, so the overall level is $\alpha$.

stem: What alternative hypothesis does the Jonckheere-Terpstra test detect?
correct: An ordering of the groups, $F_1\ge F_2\ge\cdots\ge F_k$ with at least one strict inequality, in a direction stated beforehand.
A monotone trend across ordered groups that was specified before the data were seen.

distractors.text: Any difference among the groups, in any pattern, exactly like the Kruskal-Wallis test.
A difference in variability that increases with the group index.
distractors.misconception: confuses a location trend with a scale trend

distractors.text: Equality of the group medians against all unordered alternatives.
A linear relation between group index and the mean, assuming normal errors.
A difference between the first and last groups only, ignoring the groups between.

explanation: JT is built for the ordered alternative $\mu_1\le\mu_2\le\cdots\le\mu_k$ and is more powerful than Kruskal-Wallis when the stated order is right.

stem: What is the Jonckheere-Terpstra statistic?
correct: Add, over pairs of groups, the cross-group pairs in the hypothesised order.
The sum of the pairwise Mann-Whitney counts.

distractors.text: The sum of the group rank sums weighted by the group index.
The largest Mann-Whitney statistic among all pairs of groups.
distractors.misconception: takes a maximum instead of a sum

distractors.text: The Kruskal-Wallis statistic computed on the group means.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the omnibus statistic

distractors.text: The number of observations that exceed the overall median of the pooled data.
The sum of squared differences between group mean ranks and $(N+1)/2$.
distractors.misconception: describes the sum of squares behind Kruskal-Wallis

explanation: $JT=\sum_{i<j}T_{ij}$ with $T_{ij}$ the Mann-Whitney count for groups $i$ and $j$. It ranges from $0$ to $\sum_{i<j}n_in_j$, and large values support the increasing order.

stem: What does the sign test use in a paired design?
correct: Only the signs of the differences; under the null the count is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,1/2)$.
The number of positive nonzero differences.

distractors.text: The sizes of the differences, ranked from smallest to largest.
The mean of the differences divided by its standard error.
The sum of the squared differences.
The count of differences larger than one standard deviation.
The sign of the sample mean only.

explanation: Zero differences are discarded. The test is for the median of the differences being zero, and needs no symmetry.

stem: How does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test use the differences?
correct: It ranks absolute differences and sums the ranks of the positive ones.
It combines signs with ranks of magnitudes.

distractors.text: It ranks the raw differences from smallest to largest, ignoring signs.
distractors.misconception: ignores the absolute values and signs

distractors.text: It counts only the signs.
It adds the positive differences themselves.
distractors.misconception: uses the values instead of ranks

distractors.text: It compares the group means.
It uses the ranks of the observations from both groups pooled.

explanation: $W^+=\sum_iR_i\mathbf 1\{d_i>0\}$ with $R_i$ the rank of $|d_i|$. It needs the differences to be symmetric about the median under $H_0$.

stem: Under $H_0$, what are the mean and variance of the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic $W^+$ for $n$ nonzero differences (no ties)?
correct: Mean $n(n+1)/4$ and variance $n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$.

distractors.text: Mean $n/2$ and variance $n/4$.
Mean $n(n+1)/2$ and variance $n(n+1)(2n+1)/6$.
distractors.misconception: gives the moments of the total of ranks

distractors.text: Mean $n(n+1)/4$ and variance $n^2/12$.
Mean $0$ and variance $n$.
distractors.misconception: gives the moments of a normal statistic

distractors.text: Mean $n^2/4$ and variance $n^2/24$.

explanation: Each rank $i$ is included with probability $1/2$, so $EW^+=\tfrac12\sum i=n(n+1)/4$ and $\operatorname{Var}=\tfrac14\sum i^2=n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$.

stem: Which assumption does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test need that the sign test does not?
correct: The differences are symmetric about their median.
Symmetry under the null.

distractors.text: The differences are normally distributed.
The two samples have equal variances.
The observations are independent, which the sign test does not need.
The sample is large.
distractors.misconception: describes an approximation, not an assumption

distractors.text: The data are discrete.

explanation: Without symmetry, a significant signed-rank result may reflect skewness rather than a nonzero median.

stem: What is the treatment of zero differences and ties in the signed-rank test?
correct: Zeros are dropped, ties get average ranks.
Mid-ranks for ties.

distractors.text: Zeros are given the largest rank.
Zeros count as positive differences.
Ties are broken at random in all cases.
Tied observations are always deleted.
Zeros and ties need no special handling.

explanation: With ties, the variance of $W^+$ is reduced by a correction, and exact tables no longer apply.

stem: What is the Friedman test used for?
correct: Comparing $k$ treatments on the same blocks, ranking within blocks.
A rank analogue of two-way ANOVA.

distractors.text: Comparing $k$ independent groups.
Comparing two independent samples.
Testing for rank correlation between two variables.
Testing whether data follow a distribution.
Estimating a density.

explanation: The statistic $\frac{12}{bk(k+1)}\sum_jR_j^2-3b(k+1)$ uses rank sums $R_j$ across blocks and is approximately $\chi^2_{k-1}$.

stem: How does the Friedman test differ from the Kruskal-Wallis test?
correct: Friedman ranks within blocks; Kruskal-Wallis ranks pooled data.
Related versus independent samples.

distractors.text: Friedman ranks the pooled data across all subjects.
Kruskal-Wallis ranks within blocks.
Both are for independent samples.
Friedman needs normal data.
They give identical statistics.

explanation: A block is a subject measured under every treatment; ranking within it removes subject-to-subject differences.

stem: How does Page's test differ from Friedman's test in a randomized complete block design?
correct: Page's test uses $\sum iR_{i+}$ for a specified order, so it is more powerful when that order is right.
It targets an ordered alternative; Friedman's looks for any difference.

distractors.text: Page's test ranks across blocks while Friedman's test ranks within blocks.
Page's test needs normally distributed data but Friedman's test does not.
Page's test applies to two treatments only, while Friedman's handles any number.
distractors.misconception: restricts Page's test to two treatments

distractors.text: Page's test is more powerful whatever the true ordering of the treatments turns out to be.
distractors.misconception: ignores the cost of a wrongly specified order

distractors.text: Page's test has no permutation null distribution and uses only a normal approximation.

explanation: Page's statistic weights the rank sums by the hypothesised order. If the true order is different it can have lower power than Friedman's test.

stem: When is Cochran's $Q$ test used?
correct: For several matched treatments with $0/1$ responses; it is Friedman's test with ties.
With only two treatments it reduces to McNemar's test for paired binary data.

distractors.text: For continuous responses in independent groups, as a replacement for Kruskal-Wallis.
To measure the correlation between two binary variables across subjects.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a correlation measure

distractors.text: For ordered alternatives with binary data, in the way that Page's test works.
To test the agreement of several judges who each rank the same items.
For two independent samples of binary data, as a rank-sum alternative.

explanation: With $0/1$ data within each block the ranks have heavy ties; Friedman's statistic with ties then equals Cochran's $Q$. With $k=2$ treatments it equals McNemar's test.

stem: What does Kendall's coefficient of concordance $W$ measure?
correct: The agreement among judges ranking the same items, from $0$ (none) to $1$ (perfect).
A scaling of the Friedman statistic, $W=FM/\{b(k-1)\}$.

distractors.text: The correlation between two judges' rankings, which lies between $-1$ and $1$.
distractors.misconception: confuses W with a pairwise rank correlation

distractors.text: The difference between the largest and smallest rank sum among the items.
distractors.misconception: uses a range of rank sums

distractors.text: The agreement between one judge's ranking and the true ranking of the items.
A coefficient that equals $-1$ when the judges completely disagree.
The probability that all judges choose the same best item.

explanation: With $b$ judges (blocks) and $k$ items, $W=\dfrac{12\sum(R_{i+}-b(k+1)/2)^2}{b^2k(k^2-1)}$. It is $1$ if all judges give identical rankings and near $0$ if the rank sums are nearly equal.

stem: How is Spearman's rank correlation computed?
correct: The Pearson correlation between the ranks.
Rank each variable, then correlate the ranks.

distractors.text: As the Pearson correlation of the raw values.
As the number of concordant pairs minus discordant pairs, divided by the total.
As the correlation between the signs of the values.
As the slope of the regression of ranks on values.
As the average of the ranks of the two variables.
distractors.misconception: gives a mean, not a correlation

explanation: $d_i$ is the difference between the two ranks of observation $i$. $\rho_S=\pm1$ for any strictly monotone relation.

stem: Which relationship does a rank correlation detect that the Pearson correlation may miss?
correct: A monotone but nonlinear relationship.
Any monotone association.

distractors.text: A relationship that is not monotone, such as a U shape.
A causal relationship.
A linear relationship only.
Independence between the variables.
Only perfect relationships.

explanation: For $y=e^x$ on $x=1,\dots,10$ the rank correlation is exactly 1, while Pearson's is noticeably smaller. Both are near 0 for $y=x^2$ on a symmetric $x$ range.

stem: What does the Pearson correlation coefficient measure, and what limits it?
correct: Linear association only; a monotone but curved relation can have a correlation well below $1$.
The strength of a straight-line relation, sensitive to outliers.

distractors.text: Any monotone association, so it equals $1$ for every increasing relation between the variables.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a rank correlation

distractors.text: Association between ranks, so it is unaffected by extreme observations.
Dependence of any form, so a zero Pearson correlation implies that the variables are independent.
The slope of the least squares line, which is the same number as the correlation.
distractors.misconception: confuses the slope with the correlation

distractors.text: Association only when both variables are normal, otherwise the coefficient is undefined.
distractors.misconception: thinks it needs normality to be defined

explanation: Pearson's $r$ measures linear association. An outlier can change it a lot, and $y=e^x$ on a wide range gives $r<1$ although the relation is perfectly monotone.

stem: How does a test of independence based on Spearman's coefficient work?
correct: Under independence all pairings of ranks are equally likely, so its null law depends on $n$ only.
Its null law depends on $n$ only; $\rho_S\sqrt{n-1}$ is roughly normal.

distractors.text: It assumes bivariate normality and refers $\rho_S$ to a $t$ distribution.
distractors.misconception: assumes normality for a rank statistic

distractors.text: It tests whether the means of the two variables are equal, using the ranks.
Its null distribution depends on the marginal distributions of both variables.
It is valid only when $n>100$, using a chi-square approximation.
distractors.misconception: thinks only a large-sample version exists

distractors.text: It tests whether the Pearson correlation of the raw data is exactly zero.

explanation: Under independence every pairing of ranks is equally likely, so the null distribution of $\rho_S$ depends on $n$ only; for moderate $n$, $\rho_S\sqrt{n-1}$ is approximately standard normal.

stem: What happens to Spearman's and Kendall's coefficients if one variable is transformed by a strictly increasing function?
correct: They are unchanged, since the ranks are the same.
Both are invariant to monotone increasing transformations.

distractors.text: They change in proportion to the transformation.
They become exactly 1.
They change sign.
distractors.misconception: is true only for decreasing transformations

distractors.text: They are unchanged only for linear transformations.
They are unchanged only for log transformations.

explanation: A strictly decreasing transformation reverses the ranks and changes the sign of the coefficients. Pearson's correlation is only invariant to linear maps.

stem: How is Kendall's tau defined?
correct: $(C-D)/\{n(n-1)/2\}$, concordant minus discordant.
Concordance probability minus discordance.

distractors.text: The Pearson correlation of the ranks.
The number of concordant pairs divided by $n$.
The sum of squared rank differences.
$C/D$, the ratio of concordant to discordant pairs.
The largest rank difference.

explanation: A pair $(i,j)$ is concordant if $(x_i-x_j)(y_i-y_j)>0$. Tau has a direct probabilistic meaning, unlike rho.

stem: Which statement describes the Mann-Kendall statistic $S$ for observations $x_1,\dots,x_n$ recorded in time order?
correct: $S=\sum_{i<j}\mathrm{sgn}(x_j-x_i)$, the number of rising pairs minus falling pairs.
It is Kendall's concordance statistic between the series and its time index.

distractors.text: It sums only the signs of consecutive differences $x_{t+1}-x_t$, ignoring pairs far apart in time.
distractors.misconception: uses adjacent pairs instead of all pairs

distractors.text: It sums the raw differences $x_j-x_i$ over all pairs, so large jumps dominate the value.
It tests only for a straight-line trend and needs normally distributed errors.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the regression slope test

distractors.text: It equals $n$ times the Spearman correlation between the series and time.
distractors.misconception: mixes up two different rank statistics

distractors.text: It is large only if the series rises in every single period, with no falls at all.
distractors.misconception: demands strict monotonicity period by period

explanation: Every pair $i<j$ contributes $\pm1$ according to the direction of change, so $S$ is the numerator of Kendall's tau between time and the observation. It detects monotone, not just linear, trends.

stem: Under the hypothesis that $n$ observations are iid with no ties, what are the null mean and variance of the Mann-Kendall statistic $S$?
correct: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(2n+5)/18$, with $S$ near normal for moderate $n$.
Centred at zero with variance $n(n-1)(2n+5)/18$, so a normal approximation applies.

distractors.text: $E[S]=n(n-1)/4$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(2n+5)/18$, with $S$ near normal for large $n$.
distractors.misconception: takes the mean of the concordant count rather than of $S$

distractors.text: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$, the same as the signed-rank statistic.
$E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)/2$, since there are that many pair signs.
distractors.misconception: treats the pair signs as independent

distractors.text: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(2n+5)/72$, as for the number of concordant pairs.
distractors.misconception: uses the variance of the concordant count instead of that of $S$

distractors.text: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(n+1)/12$, the same form as the rank-sum variance.
distractors.misconception: borrows the form of the rank-sum variance

explanation: $S=2C-n(n-1)/2$ where $C$ counts concordant pairs, so $\mathrm{Var}(S)=4\mathrm{Var}(C)$. Check $n=3$: $S$ takes values $\pm3,\pm1$ with probabilities $1,2,2,1$ over 6, so the variance is $22/6=3\cdot2\cdot11/18$.

stem: How are Kendall's $\tau$ and Spearman's $\rho_S$ related for the same data?
correct: Both detect monotone association and agree in sign, but $|\tau|$ is usually smaller than $|\rho_S|$.
They agree in sign for a clear trend, with $\tau$ the smaller in size.

distractors.text: They are always equal, because both are rank correlations of the same pair of variables.
distractors.misconception: assumes both coefficients take the same value

distractors.text: Kendall's $\tau$ is always larger in size than Spearman's $\rho_S$.
They can have opposite signs even when the data show a clear monotone trend.
distractors.misconception: thinks signs disagree under a clear trend

distractors.text: Kendall's $\tau$ equals $\rho_S^2$, in the same way that $R^2$ is the squared correlation.
Kendall's $\tau$ ignores the order of the observations entirely and uses only their magnitudes.

explanation: For normal data $\tau=\tfrac2\pi\arcsin\rho$ while Spearman's $\rho_S\approx\tfrac6\pi\arcsin(\rho/2)$; both are monotone in $\rho$ and $|\tau|<|\rho_S|$ except at $0,\pm1$.

stem: What does a significantly positive Mann-Kendall statistic indicate for a time series?
correct: An upward monotone trend: later values exceed earlier ones more often than chance allows.
Concordant (time, value) pairs outnumber discordant ones.

distractors.text: A linear trend with positive slope in the mean, as would be found by regression on time.
distractors.misconception: confuses a monotone trend with a linear one

distractors.text: That the series is positively serially correlated at lag one.
That the variance of the series increases over time.
distractors.misconception: confuses trend in level with trend in variance

distractors.text: That the series has a seasonal pattern that repeats from year to year.
That the first half of the data has a larger mean than the second half.

explanation: $S=\sum_{i<j}\mathrm{sign}(x_j-x_i)$ is Kendall's $\tau$ between the series and time; a large positive $S$ means pairs are mostly increasing.

stem: What is the nonparametric bootstrap?
correct: Resample with replacement and recompute the statistic each time.
Treat the empirical distribution as the population.

distractors.text: Draw new samples from a fitted normal distribution.
Resample without replacement, leaving out one observation at a time.
Split the sample into two halves.
Permute the group labels.
Increase the sample size by repeating the data.

explanation: The bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of the bootstrap replicates $\hat\theta^*_1,\dots,\hat\theta^*_B$.

stem: How is a percentile bootstrap confidence interval formed?
correct: The $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$ quantiles of the replicates.
The middle $1-\alpha$ of sorted estimates.

distractors.text: Add and subtract $1.96$ standard errors from the estimate.
Use the extreme minimum and maximum of the replicates.
Take the quantiles of the original data.
distractors.misconception: uses the sample, not the replicates

distractors.text: Use the standard error from the formula for the mean.
Take the mean of the replicates plus and minus one.

explanation: The percentile interval is transformation-respecting; BCa refines it by correcting for bias and skewness.

stem: In a sample of size $n$, what is the probability that a given observation does not appear in a bootstrap resample?
correct: $(1-1/n)^n$, about $e^{-1}\approx0.368$ for large $n$, so roughly a third is left out.
Each draw misses it with probability $1-1/n$.

distractors.text: $1/n$, the chance that one particular draw picks it.
distractors.misconception: gives the probability of a single draw

distractors.text: One half, since each observation is equally likely to be in or out.
$1-1/n^2$, because pairs of draws are independent.
Exactly zero, since resampling uses all the data.
$(1/n)^n$, the chance of drawing it every time.
distractors.misconception: gives the probability of drawing it every time

explanation: The remaining 63% of observations appear at least once; this is why out-of-bag error is based on roughly a third of the trees in bagging.

stem: How are the bootstrap standard error and bias of $\hat\theta$ estimated from replicates $\hat\theta^*_1,\dots,\hat\theta^*_B$?
correct: The SE is the standard deviation of the replicates, and the bias is their mean minus $\hat\theta$.
SE: replicate spread; bias: replicate mean minus $\hat\theta$.

distractors.text: The standard error is the range of the replicates and the bias is their median.
distractors.misconception: uses the range and the median

distractors.text: The standard error is $\hat\theta/\sqrt B$ and the bias is zero by construction.
distractors.misconception: applies a formula for a mean to any statistic

distractors.text: The bias is the replicate mean minus the true $\theta$, which becomes known after resampling.
The standard error is the standard deviation of the original data divided by $\sqrt n$ in every case.
The bias is the standard deviation of the replicates divided by $\sqrt B$.
distractors.misconception: confuses bias with Monte Carlo error

explanation: The bootstrap mimics sampling from $F$ by resampling from $\hat F_n$: the replicates $\hat\theta^*_b$ play the role of repeated estimates, so their standard deviation estimates the SE and their mean minus $\hat\theta$ estimates the bias.

stem: How does the basic (residual) bootstrap interval differ from the percentile interval?
correct: It reflects the percentile interval about $\hat\theta$, so the two differ for skewed replicates.
It uses $\hat\theta^*-\hat\theta$ as a stand-in for $\hat\theta-\theta$.

distractors.text: They are always identical, whatever the shape of the distribution of the replicates.
The basic interval is the normal interval with a bias correction added to the end points.
The basic interval uses the $\alpha$ and $1-\alpha$ percentiles in place of $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$.
It is the percentile interval that is reflected about $\hat\theta$, and the basic interval is not.
The basic interval needs a second bootstrap inside each resample to estimate a standard error.

explanation: The residual (basic) method treats $\delta^*_b=\hat\theta^*_b-\hat\theta$ as a stand-in for $\hat\theta-\theta$, giving $[\,2\hat\theta-\hat\theta^*_{1-\alpha/2},\,2\hat\theta-\hat\theta^*_{\alpha/2}]$; the percentile interval uses the replicate percentiles directly.

stem: Why use a studentised (bootstrap-$t$) interval rather than a percentile interval?
correct: The studentised statistic is nearly pivotal, so its bootstrap distribution gives more accurate coverage.
A pivot's law does not depend on the unknown parameter.

distractors.text: It needs no standard error, so it is cheaper to compute than the percentile interval.
distractors.misconception: forgets that each resample needs a standard error

distractors.text: It is invariant to monotone transformations of the parameter, unlike the percentile interval.
distractors.misconception: attributes the percentile property to the bootstrap-t

distractors.text: It always gives a shorter interval than the percentile interval for the same data.
It guarantees exactly the nominal coverage for every sample size and every distribution.
It removes the need to resample, because the studentised statistic has a known distribution.
distractors.misconception: thinks the pivot has a known null distribution

explanation: Studentising by $SE^*_b$ makes the statistic nearly pivotal. This is usually more accurate than percentile or normal intervals, at the cost of a standard error for every resample.

stem: In the bootstrap-$t$ interval for a mean, which percentiles of the $t^*_b$ values are used, and how?
correct: The interval is $\bar x-t^*_{1-\alpha/2}S/\sqrt n$ to $\bar x-t^*_{\alpha/2}S/\sqrt n$, upper percentile first.
The $t^*_b$ percentiles replace $t$ quantiles, in reversed order.

distractors.text: $\bar x+t^*_{\alpha/2}S/\sqrt n$ to $\bar x+t^*_{1-\alpha/2}S/\sqrt n$, with the percentiles in the same order.
The percentiles of the bootstrap means $\bar x^*_b$ are taken directly.
Percentiles of $t^*_b$ are used with the standard error $S/\sqrt n$ replaced by $S$.
The median of the $t^*_b$ is the centre, and the half-width comes from their quartiles.
The single percentile $t^*_{1-\alpha/2}$ is used on both sides, giving a symmetric interval.

explanation: The pivot is $t=(\bar X-\mu)/(S/\sqrt n)$. Solving $t^*_{\alpha/2}<t<t^*_{1-\alpha/2}$ for $\mu$ reverses the order of the percentiles.

stem: What problem does the BCa interval address?
correct: Bias and skewness in the bootstrap distribution, handled by shifting the percentile levels used.
A biased estimator whose standard error changes with the parameter.

distractors.text: Dependence among the observations of the original sample.
Small values of $B$, which it replaces by an analytic formula for the interval.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a Monte Carlo accuracy fix

distractors.text: Nothing that the percentile interval does not already handle, apart from transformations.
Non-normality of the data, which it removes by transforming the observations first.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with transforming the data

distractors.text: The need for a standard error, which it removes by using only order statistics.

explanation: BCa corrects the percentile levels for a bias constant $z_0$ and an acceleration constant $a$, giving better coverage when the estimator is biased or its variance depends on the parameter.

stem: In the BCa interval, what do the constants $z_0$ and $a$ represent?
correct: $z_0$ measures median bias of the replicates and $a$ the acceleration of the standard error.
$z_0$ is a bias constant and $a$ an acceleration constant.

distractors.text: $z_0$ is the critical value of the test and $a$ is its significance level.
$z_0$ is the mean of the replicates and $a$ is exactly their skewness.
$a$ is the bias constant and $z_0$ is the acceleration constant.
distractors.misconception: swaps the roles of the constants

distractors.text: Both constants equal the number of bootstrap resamples used.
Both constants are $0$ whenever the data themselves are symmetric.
distractors.misconception: thinks symmetric data force zero constants

explanation: $\hat z_0=\Phi^{-1}\big(\#\{\hat\theta^*_b<\hat\theta\}/B\big)$ and $\hat a$ is estimated from the jackknife; the interval ends are percentiles at levels $\Phi\big(z_0+\frac{z_0+z}{1-a(z_0+z)}\big)$.

stem: When $z_0=0$ and $a=0$, what does the BCa interval reduce to?
correct: The percentile interval, with the $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$ percentiles.
The plain percentile interval from the replicates.

distractors.text: The normal-based interval $\hat\theta\pm z_{\alpha/2}\widehat{SE}$.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the normal interval

distractors.text: The basic (residual) interval reflected about $\hat\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the basic interval

distractors.text: The bootstrap-$t$ interval based on studentised replicates.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the studentised interval

distractors.text: An empty interval, because the adjusted levels coincide.
The interval from the smallest to the largest of the $B$ replicates.

explanation: With $z_0=a=0$ the adjusted level is $\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$ (and $1-\alpha/2$ for the upper end), which are the percentile levels.

stem: What is resampled in the paired (case) bootstrap for a regression?
correct: Whole observations $(x_i,y_i)$ are drawn with replacement and the regression is refitted.
Pairs are drawn together, so the predictor values also change from resample to resample.

distractors.text: Only the residuals, with the original $x_i$ values kept fixed.
Only the $y$ values, with the $x$ values kept in their original order.
The fitted values, which are then refitted by least squares.
The regression coefficients themselves, drawn from their estimated sampling distribution.
distractors.misconception: confuses the bootstrap with a parametric simulation

distractors.text: The $x$ values only, with new $y$ values generated from the fitted model.

explanation: In the paired bootstrap each resample is a set of $n$ pairs drawn with replacement; the regression is refitted to get $\hat\beta^*$.

stem: How does the residual bootstrap build a resample for a regression?
correct: Fit, resample the residuals, form $y^*_i=\hat y_i+e^*_i$ with $x_i$ fixed, and refit.
Fitted values plus resampled residuals, with the design fixed.

distractors.text: Draw pairs with replacement and add normal noise to the responses.
distractors.misconception: mixes the paired bootstrap with a parametric step

distractors.text: Permute the $x$ values among the observations and refit the line.
distractors.misconception: describes a permutation test for the slope

distractors.text: Draw new residuals from a normal distribution with the estimated error variance.
Resample the $y$ values and keep the residuals fixed at their original positions.
distractors.misconception: swaps the roles of responses and residuals

distractors.text: Remove one observation at a time and refit the model each time.

explanation: The residual bootstrap treats the fitted values as fixed and resamples the residuals: $y^*_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i+e^*_i$. It assumes exchangeable (homoscedastic) errors.

stem: How is a bootstrap hypothesis test carried out?
correct: Resample from data adjusted so that $H_0$ holds, and take the share of statistics at least as extreme as observed.
The null distribution comes from resampling under $H_0$, not from the raw data.

distractors.text: Resample from the original data without any adjustment and compare the replicates with zero.
Reject whenever the bootstrap confidence interval contains the observed statistic.
Use the bootstrap standard error with the normal table, with no resampling under $H_0$.
distractors.misconception: turns it into a Wald test

distractors.text: Permute the group labels without replacement; that permutation test is the bootstrap test.
Count the proportion of replicates below $t_{\text{obs}}$ whatever the direction of the alternative.

explanation: The resampling must reflect $H_0$ (for example shifting each group to a common mean). The p-value is $\#\{t^*_b\ge t_{\text{obs}}\}/B$, or $(1+\#)/(B+1)$.

stem: Why does the bootstrap perform poorly for the sample maximum?
correct: A resample contains the observed maximum with probability $1-(1-1/n)^n\approx0.63$, giving a large atom there.
The maximum is not smooth in the data, so the bootstrap does not mimic its law.

distractors.text: The maximum has no finite variance, so no resampling method can estimate it.
distractors.misconception: thinks the maximum has infinite variance

distractors.text: $B$ would have to exceed $n^n$ before the resamples reach extreme values.
distractors.misconception: invents a size condition on B

distractors.text: The bootstrap needs normal data, and the maximum of a sample is never normal.
Resampling cannot produce values larger than the sample mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses the maximum with the mean

distractors.text: The bootstrap fails for every order statistic, including the sample median, by the same mechanism.
distractors.misconception: overgeneralises the failure to all order statistics

explanation: For the sample maximum of a continuous distribution the bootstrap distribution has mass $1-(1-1/n)^n\to1-e^{-1}$ at $X_{(n)}$, but the true distribution has no atom.

stem: When is the paired bootstrap preferable to the residual bootstrap in regression?
correct: When the error variance may depend on $x$ or the model may be misspecified.
When predictors are random and errors depend on $x$.

distractors.text: When the predictors are fixed by the design and the residuals are exchangeable.
distractors.misconception: describes the case that favours the residual bootstrap

distractors.text: Never, because the residual bootstrap is always at least as accurate.
distractors.misconception: claims the residual bootstrap always wins

distractors.text: Only when the sample size is below five.
Only when the regression has no intercept term.
Only when the response is binary, because pairs then have a binomial distribution.

explanation: The residual bootstrap assumes exchangeable errors; the paired bootstrap makes weaker assumptions and so is more robust to heteroscedasticity or an incorrect model.

stem: How does the jackknife estimate the bias of a statistic $\hat\theta$?
correct: $(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)$, from leave-one-out estimates.
Compare the full estimate with leave-one-out averages.

distractors.text: $\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta$, without the factor $n-1$.
As the standard deviation of the leave-one-out estimates.
As the difference between the mean and the median of the data.
By resampling with replacement many times.
It cannot estimate bias.

explanation: The jackknife-corrected estimate is $n\hat\theta-(n-1)\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}$, which removes the $O(1/n)$ bias.

stem: Where does the jackknife fail?
correct: For non-smooth statistics such as the median.
Sample quantiles are not smooth functions.

distractors.text: For the sample mean.
distractors.misconception: the jackknife works well for the mean

distractors.text: For linear statistics.
distractors.misconception: the jackknife works well for smooth statistics

distractors.text: For any statistic when the sample size is above 100.
For smooth functions of means.
Whenever the data are normal.

explanation: Bootstrap works for the median; neither works for the sample maximum.

stem: How does the jackknife estimate the standard error of $\hat\theta$?
correct: From the leave-one-out estimates, $\sqrt{\tfrac{n-1}n\sum(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar\theta_{(\cdot)})^2}$.
By a scaled spread of the $n$ leave-one-out estimates about their mean, with factor $(n-1)/n$.

distractors.text: By the sample standard deviation of the original data divided by $\sqrt n$.
distractors.misconception: uses the standard error of a mean for every statistic

distractors.text: By the spread of $n$ random resamples drawn with replacement.
By $\sqrt{\tfrac1n\sum(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar\theta_{(\cdot)})^2}$ with no extra factor.
By the range of the leave-one-out estimates divided by $n$.
By the difference between the largest and the smallest leave-one-out estimate.
distractors.misconception: uses the full range as the standard error

explanation: Leave-one-out estimates vary much less than independent estimates, and the factor $(n-1)/n$ restores the scale: $\widehat{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{n-1}n\sum(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar\theta_{(\cdot)})^2}$.

stem: What is the bias-corrected jackknife estimate of $\theta$?
correct: $n\hat\theta-(n-1)\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}$, which removes the leading $1/n$ term of the bias.
The estimate minus the jackknife bias, $\hat\theta-(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)$.

distractors.text: $\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}$ itself, the average of the leave-one-out estimates.
distractors.misconception: uses the average of the leave-one-out estimates

distractors.text: $\hat\theta+(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)$, the estimate plus the jackknife bias.
distractors.misconception: adds the bias instead of subtracting it

distractors.text: $\hat\theta/(n-1)$, the estimate scaled by the leave-one-out sample size.
The median of the leave-one-out estimates, which removes the bias.
$(n-1)\hat\theta-n\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}$, with the two weights interchanged.

explanation: The jackknife bias estimate is $(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)$; subtracting it gives $n\hat\theta-(n-1)\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}$.

stem: How does the jackknife differ from the bootstrap?
correct: The jackknife is deterministic, using the $n$ leave-one-out samples; the bootstrap resamples at random.
The jackknife needs $n$ recomputations but handles non-smooth statistics worse.

distractors.text: The jackknife resamples with replacement while the bootstrap leaves one observation out.
The jackknife works for the median while the bootstrap does not.
distractors.misconception: swaps which method fails for the median

distractors.text: The jackknife always needs more computation than the bootstrap.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the jackknife needs only n recomputations

distractors.text: They give identical standard errors for every statistic and every data set.
